item.title: Quantum Error Correction in Nearly Critical Toric Codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that topological error‑correction can remain robust even as a toric code is driven right up to its quantum critical point, demonstrating a finite decoding threshold for both bit‑flip and phase‑flip noise when the transverse field is infinitesimally close to the transition. By exploiting the stoquastic nature of the transverse‑field toric Hamiltonian, the authors devise an optimal post‑measurement decoder that can be implemented efficiently with Monte Carlo simulations of a constrained lattice gauge theory—an approach that bridges quantum many‑body physics and practical fault‑tolerance. The result suggests that future quantum memories could tolerate stronger perturbations than previously thought, though the technique currently applies only to stoquastic deformations of stabilizer codes.

We investigate quantum error correction protocols for topological codes deformed away from their stabilizer limits, particularly as they are pushed towards quantum phase transitions into trivial phases. Our focus is primarily on quantum information stored within the ground-state manifold of the transverse-field toric code (TFTC), subjected to independent bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence. Although the transverse field induces strong quantum fluctuations of $m$ anyons in the ground states, we show that projective measurements of the "bare" toric code stabilizers can nevertheless be used to construct an efficient decoding algorithm which exhibits a finite threshold to both types of decoherence, even when the transverse field is tuned infinitesimally close to the quantum critical point. Our construction of the optimal postmeasurement decoders---that is, the optimal decoders assuming that the stabilizers are first measured---crucially relies on the stoquastic nature of the TFTC Hamiltonian, which affords a description of its ground states in terms of a classical lattice gauge theory. Using stoquasticity, we first prove that stabilizer measurements act unitarily on the undecohered TFTC ground states to excellent approximation, and that the optimal postmeasurement decoder can be efficiently implemented via Monte Carlo simulation of a constrained lattice gauge theory. We then construct the optimal postmeasurement decoder for the TFTC states under bit-flip and phase-flip decoherence, where we numerically demonstrate a finite threshold close to the quantum critical point. We provide theoretical evidence (without a rigorous proof) that stabilizer measurements constitute an optimal decoding strategy in this setting. For phase-flip decoherence, we further prove that the optimal postmeasurement decoding threshold is independent of the transverse field strength throughout the topological phase.

item.title: Quantum Advantage has Few Complexity Implications
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the existence of “proofs of quantumness” or oblivious state‑preparation protocols does not automatically force a separation between classical and quantum complexity classes, even in worlds where P = NP or BQP = QCMA. By constructing explicit classical and unitary oracles, the authors demonstrate that such quantum advantage tests can coexist with surprisingly weak separations, which tempers expectations that they will directly yield new post‑quantum cryptographic primitives via relativizing proofs. The result sharpens our understanding of what recent experimental demonstrations of quantumness can (and cannot) guarantee for future security constructions.

We consider the complexity implications of proofs of quantumness and (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation. We show that both of these objects can coexist with the easiness of nondeterministic computation. That is, we give evidence that proofs of quantumness can exist when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{NP}$ and that (quantum verifier) oblivious state preparation can exist when $\mathsf{BQP} = \mathsf{QCMA}$. In particular, we give a classical oracle relative to which (1) $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{NP}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{PSPACE}^\mathcal{O}$ (3) Proofs of quantumness exist. In particular, there exists a language in $\mathsf{IP}^\mathcal{O} \subseteq \mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O}$ which is hard on average against $\mathsf{P}^\mathcal{O}/poly$. We give a unitary oracle such that (1) $\mathsf{BQP}^\mathcal{O} = \mathsf{QCMA}^\mathcal{O}$ (2) Quantum verifier oblivious state preparation exists. These oracle separations directly imply a number of related consequences. For example, our first result implies that proofs of quantumness cannot be used to construct classical or quantum cryptography with a relativizing proof. Our second result implies that quantum computation/classical communication oblivious transfer cannot be used to construct post-quantum one-way functions with a relativizing proof.

item.title: DynaMite: Dynamic Measurement Scheduling To Accelerate Fault-Tolerant Quantum Programs
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article tackles one of the biggest hidden bottlenecks in fault‑tolerant processors: the static measurement latency that inflates logical cycle times and error rates. By introducing DynaMite’s real‑time latency selection, which tailors readout speed to each logical cycle’s error budget, the authors show a clear path to shave tens of percent off both runtime and logical error probability—an advance that dovetails with recent efforts in active reset and low‑latency control stacks from IBM and Google. If hardware can expose fast, programmable measurement windows, the technique could become a practical lever for scaling up surface‑code or other QEC codes without waiting for fundamentally faster detectors.

Fault-tolerant quantum computers run millions of logical cycles to perform quantum error correction (QEC). As logical operations span entire logical cycles, the logical cycle time (LCT) dictates program runtime. Qubit measurements, critical to extract parity information for QEC, are the slowest operations and account for 43-86% of LCT. Measurement latencies impact fidelity: fast measurements lower our ability to correctly classify quantum states, whereas slow measurements increase the likelihood of decoherence. Hardware providers thus calibrate measurement latencies that maximize readout fidelity per qubit and use them to schedule all measurements during program execution. However, calibrated latencies are sub-optimal for logical performance because logical cycles span multiple QEC rounds, during which data qubits are not measured. This increases LCT and logical error rates (LERs) due to decoherence at the logical level. We propose DynaMite, a lightweight real-time measurement latency selection policy built on two key insights. First, logical cycles must use a measurement latency that is fast enough to reduce both LCT and LER for the QEC code, instead of the calibrated latency that only maximizes readout fidelity. Second, not all logical cycles are equal; many do not fully utilize the error budget of the QEC code, i.e., the number of failed parity checks it can tolerate without compromising LER. These cycles could use even faster measurements but do not, because latencies are chosen statically, whereas error information is only available at runtime. DynaMite exploits the fact that a logical cycle comprises multiple QEC rounds and selects the fastest latency for an upcoming round based on the error budget left and rounds remaining. Our evaluations show that DynaMite reduces LCT by 1.69x on average and up to 2.29x, and reduces LER to 0.46x on average and up to 0.13x of baseline.

item.title: Data informed Ansatz Selection for Variational Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This work shows that the architecture of variational quantum circuits can be chosen deterministically from the data itself rather than by costly trial‑and‑error searches, a step that could dramatically shrink the overhead of VQC design on near‑term hardware. By linking Fourier coefficient ranks to entanglement needs and using the growth law of the quantum Fisher information matrix to set depth, the authors provide concrete, analytically grounded rules that complement recent efforts to automate ansatz construction and reduce barren‑plateau risk. The demonstrated 78 % accuracy on a benchmark dataset without any hyperparameter sweep suggests a practical pathway for scaling VQCs to larger problems while keeping experimental resources in check, though performance will still depend on the quality of data encoding and hardware noise levels.

Choosing a variational quantum circuit (VQC) usually means searching over ansatze and depths, and training each candidate. We give three rules that fix these choices from the data and the gate set alone, before any training. First, a circuit without entangling gates has a rank-one Fourier coefficient tensor on every subset of qubits. A singular value decomposition of a dataset's Fourier coefficients therefore indicates whether entanglement is needed, which qubits it connects, and a lower bound on the error of omitting it. Second, the rank of the quantum Fisher information matrix grows by $p_0$ per layer, after a first-layer deficit $d_0$, until it reaches a ceiling set by the dynamical Lie algebra. This law fixes the depth. Third, reading out all $2^N - 1$ Pauli-Z products from one batch of shots resolves half of the state's directions, the most any single-basis readout can. A single-qubit readout resolves an exponentially small fraction. For the Madelon dataset, the rules prescribe 7 blocks of 3 qubits at depth 3: a 239-parameter classifier with 78.5% test accuracy, found without a grid search. Ablations confirm three predicted effects: shallower circuits, smaller blocks and dropping reuploading all lower accuracy.

item.title: QECert: Formal Foundations for Quantum Error-Correction Theory in Lean
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it brings the rigor of interactive theorem proving to quantum error‑correction theory, giving researchers a machine‑checked foundation for the increasingly complex constructions that underpin scalable fault tolerance. By encoding stabilizer, CSS and modern LDPC code families—including hypergraph‑product and quantum Tanner codes—in Lean, QECert lets developers verify asymptotic parameter bounds, Bravyi‑Poulin‑Terhal limits and magic‑state overheads with confidence, a step that aligns with the recent surge of high‑performance LDPC designs for near‑term devices. The library’s reusable formalism could accelerate both theoretical advances and practical compiler or architecture verification, though its impact will depend on broader adoption within the quantum community.

Quantum error correction provides the mathematical basis for protecting quantum information against noise. Existing formalizations have established foundations for stabilizer codes and code verification. However, a systematic formal treatment of the asymptotic constructions and fundamental limitations that underpin scalable quantum error correction is still needed. We present QECert, a Lean library providing reusable formal foundations for these theoretical questions. It connects quantum error-correction criteria, stabilizer and Calderbank-Shor-Steane codes, and algebraic and homological constructions within a common framework. Asymptotically good quantum low density parity check codes provide the principal case study. We formalize constructions and asymptotic parameter theorems spanning hypergraph products, balanced products, lifted products, and quantum Tanner codes. Further developments cover Bravyi-Poulin-Terhal bounds and related locality restrictions, constant overhead magic state distillation, and energy barriers and storage errors for quantum memories. QECert establishes a reusable formal foundation for studying the capabilities, resource requirements, and fundamental limitations of quantum error correction, supporting systematic verification and further development of its theory.

item.title: Reopening the one clean qubit case of a semi-grand challenge
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article revives a long‑standing open problem by showing that the previously accepted proof that “one clean qubit” circuits stay classically simulable is flawed, exposing a concrete counterexample that still respects full separability yet evades the claimed simulation form. By pinpointing the gap in Aaronson’s 2005 semi‑grand challenge argument, it forces theorists to re‑examine the boundary between efficiently simulable mixed‑state models and genuinely quantum advantage—an issue now especially relevant as experimental groups explore DQC1‑style processors with noisy registers. Although the new circuits themselves are easy to simulate, the work underscores that a definitive answer to whether separable mixed‑state computation can be classically tractable remains unsettled, keeping the question alive for future algorithmic and complexity‑theoretic breakthroughs.

In his 2005 list of semi-grand challenges for quantum computing theory, Scott Aaronson asked whether a quantum computer that is always in a separable mixed state can be simulated by a classical computer in polynomial time. An affirmative answer was claimed for the one clean qubit model of quantum computation. The supporting mathematical arguments relied on an exhaustive characterization of circuits that stay in separable states. Here, we give a counterexample where one pure qubit, known as the clean qubit, controls a sequence of three gates that act on a maximally mixed three-qubit register. The overall unitary that accumulates as these gates are applied has the properties that ensure the state of all four qubits remains fully separable. Crucially, we show that the final unitary cannot be put into the form required by the claimed simulation result. We also give a continuous-time implementation of the same circuit that keeps the qubits fully separable throughout and ends at the same unitary. We extend our counterexamples to a uniform family, and pinpoint the gap in the earlier proof. Since our circuits are themselves efficient to simulate classically, this work does not settle Aaronson's question. It does, however, reopen the semi-grand challenge for an actively researched model of quantum computation.

item.title: Recoverability of Gravitational Entanglement under Decoherence
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the disappearance of a measurable gravitational‑entanglement signal under realistic noise does not mean the underlying quantum resource is gone – strictly local quantum error‑correction can amplify the effective Newtonian coupling relative to residual decoherence for GRW and CSL collapse models, even when the raw entanglement appears vanishing. By contrast, the Diósi–Penrose model resists such recovery, highlighting a concrete way to discriminate between competing theories of gravity‑induced decoherence with near‑term tabletop experiments. The work therefore bridges recent proposals to witness gravity‑mediated entanglement and practical error‑mitigation techniques, suggesting that clever encoding could keep quantum‑gravity signatures alive despite environmental noise.

Decoherence can make gravitationally generated entanglement arbitrarily small, or even vanishing, without necessarily rendering the effective matter dynamics separable. We ask whether this hidden non-separability can be revealed using strictly local quantum error correction. For Newtonian gravity supplemented by physically relevant localization noise, including environmental noise, and noise from collapse models such as GRW, CSL, and Diósi--Penrose, we analyze when the underlying entangling resource is locally recoverable. For GRW- and CSL-type noise, we analytically establish that strictly local quantum error correction can make the ratio of the effective gravitational interaction strength to the residual decoherence rate arbitrarily large for any parametrization of the collapse model, even in regimes where the unencoded entanglement signal approaches zero. By contrast, the Diósi--Penrose model does not exhibit the same enhancement under bipartite protocol considered here, revealing a qualitative difference. These results show that the loss of detectable entanglement is not equivalent to the loss of a recoverable non-separable resource, and open a route toward practical recovery protocols.

item.title: FirstQFM Demonstrates Quantum Reservoir Computing on Rigetti’s 108-Qubit Processor to Outperform Classical Financial Benchmarks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows the first practical use‑case where a noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) processor can beat state‑of‑the‑art classical models on a real‑world financial forecasting task, highlighting quantum reservoir computing as a latency‑friendly way to harness large qubit arrays. By leveraging Rigetti’s 108‑qubit chip, FirstQFM demonstrates that even without full fault tolerance, quantum‑enhanced time‑series analysis can deliver higher Sharpe ratios and profit metrics than leading machine‑learning baselines. The result builds on recent work exploring hybrid quantum‑classical learning architectures and suggests a near‑term pathway for quant firms to experiment with NISQ hardware, though the advantage remains task‑specific and does not yet constitute a universal quantum speedup.

FirstQFM, in collaboration with SW7 Group and Rigetti Computing, has successfully demonstrated a financial forecasting pilot using quantum reservoir computing (QRC) on Rigetti’s 108-qubit processor. This QRC system outperformed classical machine learning models and time-series foundation models in financial benchmarks, achieving significantly higher cumulative gross profit and loss and Sharpe ratios. The study highlights QRC as a promising and latency-efficient approach for deploying NISQ processors in quantitative finance, despite not claiming general quantum advantage. item.title: Band structure of two-dimensional graphene and of one-dimensional nanoribbons via variational quantum algorithms: from energies to wavefunction quality
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a single variational workflow can map the band structure of realistic graphene sheets and nanoribbons onto current NISQ hardware, showing how VQE and its deflation extension can retrieve both ground‑state and excited‑state dispersions with only logarithmic qubit scaling. By quantifying how circuit depth trades off between ideal accuracy and noise‑induced error, the work provides a practical benchmark for future materials‑focused quantum simulations and highlights the need for deeper, lower‑error devices before truly predictive calculations become feasible.

Simulating quantum many-body systems classically encounters exponential bottlenecks, which quantum devices circumvent by natively encoding wavefunctions. In the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, however, hardware noise constrains simulation accuracy. As a stepping stone toward strongly correlated materials, we compute the band structure of 2D monolayer graphene and 1D nanoribbons (zigzag and armchair) using a single variational workflow in the $p_z$ tight-binding approximation. Non-interacting ground states also provide essential initial reference states for subspace and warm-started variational methods to solve interacting spectra. By mapping the Bloch Hamiltonian to Pauli operators, we extract the ground band via the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and excited subbands via Variational Quantum Deflation (VQD), validating our approach from ideal simulations to execution on physical IBM Quantum processors. In ideal simulations, the workflow reproduces exact diagonalization results with high precision, whereas hardware noise introduces energy deviations of a few hundredths of the hopping parameter. While qubit counts scale logarithmically with ribbon width, fixed-depth ansatz accuracy degrades with Hilbert space dimension. Crucially, deepening the ansatz improves ideal simulation accuracy by over three orders of magnitude but worsens energy estimates under noise, proving that practical circuit depth is bounded by hardware noise rather than expressivity. Finally, we complement energy evaluations with a wavefunction-level diagnostic measuring subspace containment. This diagnostic captures degenerate manifolds and exposes optimization failure modes disguised by energy agreement alone. Operating directly on NISQ hardware, this validated workflow establishes a controlled baseline for studying topological and strongly correlated phases in realistic materials.

item.title: Substantially Improved Rate and Distance for Addressable Transversal Phase Gates
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article pushes the frontier of fault‑tolerant quantum computing by delivering explicit families of error‑correcting codes that combine a higher encoding rate and larger relative distance with fully addressable transversal non‑Clifford phase gates—a rare combination that has long been limited to modest parameters. By moving beyond binary CSS constructions and using cyclic, algebraic‑geometric techniques, the authors raise the asymptotic lower bound on both rate and distance to roughly 0.077 / h and even tighten it further with an exponential‑time construction, narrowing the gap to a newly derived universal upper limit. The concrete 48‑ and 90‑qubit codes for transversal T gates give hardware designers realistic benchmarks for building more efficient logical layers while highlighting that further gains will still require clever code design or trade‑offs in compilation overhead.

An important ingredient in fault-tolerant quantum computation is asymptotically good codes with fully addressable transversal non-Clifford gates. Existing constructions, however, provide only small explicit guarantees for rate and relative distance. Here, we substantially improve these guarantees for fully addressable transversal phase gates at every fixed level $h\ge3$ of the Clifford hierarchy, using a cyclic encoding beyond the binary CSS framework. The encoding separates logical phase control from the joint design of rate and distance, enabling two constructions with different computational costs. A deterministic polynomial-time algebraic-geometric construction gives a common asymptotic lower bound of $52/(675h)$ on both quantities. A counting argument gives an exponential-time construction with exact verification, improving this bound by a factor of approximately $2.86$. We further establish a universal upper bound for codes supporting fully addressable transversal single-qubit phase gates. Within our cyclic encoding framework, we obtain a stronger upper bound that is approximately $1.28$ times the lower bound achieved by our exponential-time construction. As concrete examples, we construct codes with $48$ and $90$ physical qubits supporting fully addressable transversal $T$ gates. These results narrow the gap between achievable code parameters and addressability bounds, providing quantitative targets for further improvements in efficient code constructions.

item.title: Conditional Quantum Priors for Chaotic Fluid Dynamics
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a single quantum‑generated prior can be conditioned on system parameters such as the Reynolds number, letting classical neural networks inherit accurate long‑term statistical information without retraining for each new flow regime. By cutting the required trainable weights by roughly 85 % and halving the Jensen–Shannon divergence on Lorenz‑63, the work demonstrates a concrete efficiency boost that aligns with the broader push toward hybrid quantum‑classical machine‑learning pipelines for physics problems. The photonic NISQ implementation further proves the approach is viable on near‑term hardware, suggesting a practical route to more reliable turbulence forecasting once larger quantum devices become available.

Neural networks that predict chaotic dynamics can reproduce short trajectories while misrepresenting statistics over long times. Quantum priors represent selected dynamical statistics through quantum generative models and provide statistical constraints for classical neural networks. Training a separate prior for each value of a system parameter, such as the Reynolds number, does not explicitly model how these statistics vary with that parameter. We learn a conditional quantum prior that approximates selected statistics of an invariant measure at unseen parameter values within the training range, without retraining. For Lorenz-63, the prior reduces mean Jensen-Shannon divergence by 56.9% relative to a classical multilayer perceptron with a comparable number of weights across 96 unseen parameter values. Across 101 values of the same parameter, the shared prior uses 84.7% fewer trainable weights than would be required by a separate quantum neural network at each value. We then use the learned prior to regularize classical neural networks, encouraging their autoregressive rollouts to better reproduce long-term statistics. For Kolmogorov flow at Reynolds number $Re=1000$, prior regularization reduces forecast mean squared error by 66.0% over 318 steps relative to the classical baseline without prior regularization. We also implement a photonic quantum prior for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, achieving a mean Jensen-Shannon divergence of $4.58\times10^{-3}$ for Lorenz-63 and $2.59\times10^{-3}$ for Kolmogorov flow at unseen parameter values.

item.title: Autonomous cooling of Kerr-cat qubits to minutes-long bit-flip times
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that Kerr‑cat qubits can be autonomously cooled via a resonant lossy mode, extending their intrinsic bit‑flip lifetime from milliseconds to minutes (up to 450 s) while preserving fast Z gates and high‑fidelity single‑shot readout. By confirming the predicted exponential scaling of flip times with photon number, the work pushes biased‑noise hardware‑efficient error correction into a regime where logical qubits could be built with dramatically lower overhead than conventional superconducting transmons. The result shows that the remaining bottleneck is now phase‑flip loss rather than bit‑flips, highlighting a clear path toward more practical fault‑tolerant quantum processors.

Quantum error correction becomes more hardware efficient when physical noise is strongly biased towards one error channel. Cat qubits realize such a bias by encoding information in two opposite coherent states of a superconducting oscillator, so that bit flips are exponentially suppressed with photon number while phase-flip rates increase only linearly. In Kerr-cat qubits, a driven double-well potential confines these states and enables fast coherent control, but excitations can induce interwell switching, limiting bit-flip times to milliseconds. Here we show that the nonlinear interaction generating the confinement can also cool these excitations. When an intra-well transition becomes resonant with a lossy readout mode, excitations are transferred out of the qubit and dissipated, as established by spectroscopy and relaxation measurements. We observe the predicted exponential scaling of Kerr-cat bit-flip times with photon number, reaching 450 s, over five orders of magnitude beyond previous demonstrations. Phase-flip rates remain consistent with intrinsic photon loss at operating points with seconds-long bit-flip times. We further demonstrate fast Z gates without measurable degradation of bit-flip protection and single-shot readout with a bit-flip probability below $10^{-6}$ per measurement. Autonomous cooling thus brings minutes-long bit-flip protection to Kerr-cat qubits while retaining fast coherent control, without additional cooling drives or circuit elements.

item.title: Sleep-Disordered Breathing Detection with Quantum Recurrent Neural Networks
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a hybrid quantum‑classical recurrent network can match—and on a tiny dataset even surpass—state‑of‑the‑art classical RNNs while using orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters and only a handful of qubits, highlighting the efficiency gains possible with variational quantum models. It builds on recent advances in quantum machine learning that have shown promise for static classification tasks, extending them to real‑world time‑series data such as sleep‑disordered breathing detection. The results suggest that, once more robust hardware and error mitigation techniques become available, quantum recurrent architectures could offer compact, low‑power alternatives for edge‑deployed health monitoring and other sequential inference problems.

item.description:

Exploring interactions between quantum emitters and guided photons, waveguide quantum electrodynamics (wQED) offers a versatile platform for quantum simulation and quantum interconnect. To simplify the quantized light-matter interactions, a linearized dispersion approximation (LDA) was widely used in wQED under the conditions of weak coupling and narrow photonic bandwidth. However, a growing number of strong-coupling wQED experiments have called the validity of LDA into question. Here, by investigating giant atoms coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, we propose a principle to judge the validity of LDA. We find that the decoherence of the atoms exhibits rich dynamical behaviors determined by different numbers of bound states in and out of the continuum (BICs and BOCs) formed in the energy spectrum of the total atom-photon system. Based on this, we show that despite the LDA can partially preserve some of BICs, it completely erases BOCs. This causes the dominant role of LDA in the atomic dynamics to break down. Providing a physical insight into the validity of LDA, our results lay a firm foundation for exploring fundamental physics and its application frontier in strong-coupling wQED platforms.

item.title: Time-invariant negativity and persistent bound entanglement in a cyclic two-qutrit family
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first observation of time‑invariant entanglement in a qutrit‑qutrit pair subjected to collective dephasing, showing that a suitably weighted component in a decoherence‑free subspace can lock the negativity at a constant non‑zero value despite ongoing noise. By delivering exact PPT/ separability boundaries, explicit product decompositions and a closed‑form realignment test, the authors give the community a rare “complete” characterization of bound‑entangled trajectories that complements recent studies on decoherence‑free subspaces and entanglement sudden death. The results suggest new routes for designing noise‑resilient high‑dimensional quantum channels, although the effect hinges on precise state preparation and may be sensitive to deviations from the ideal collective dephasing model.

We study the entanglement dynamics of two qutrits under collective dephasing for a family of states obtained by mixing a maximally entangled state that lives in the decoherence-free subspace with three nonstationary two-term states sharing a common amplitude ratio $r$. We obtain exact PPT and separability regions along the whole trajectory, a specialization of known results on cyclic sign invariant states, and we supply explicit certificates: a finite product decomposition, three fixed positive-map witnesses, and a closed realignment formula that detects every PPT-entangled state, so that no state is left undecided. The negativity is computed in closed form. It shows that the entanglement is time-invariant, positive and constant from the initial time although the state changes, exactly when the weight of the maximally entangled state exceeds the threshold $U_r=r/(1+r+r^2)$. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of time-invariant entanglement for qutrit--qutrit systems under collective dephasing. For smaller weights the entanglement decays and vanishes at a finite time: the state either becomes separable (entanglement sudden death) or, for $r\neq1$ in an intermediate range, loses distillability suddenly and remains bound entangled at all later times. Every state with negative partial transpose is one-copy distillable by a fixed local projection. The same trajectories arise from the global dephasing map and from a correlated local random-unitary semigroup, although the two channels differ on product inputs. Exact rational benchmarks and embeddings of the Horodecki and Ha--Kye--Park families are provided.

item.title: Quantum channel tomography: optimal bounds in the near-boundary regime
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article finally closes the last open case in quantum channel tomography by pinning down the query complexity when the dilation rate τ is just above one, a regime that had resisted analysis despite its relevance to near‑optimal process learning. By showing that diamond‑norm tomography loses Heisenberg scaling abruptly while Choi‑trace‑norm tomography degrades smoothly, the work clarifies how resource requirements transition from quantum‑enhanced to classical limits—a nuance that will guide experimental designs for characterising noisy intermediate‑scale devices. The tight lower and upper bounds also provide a benchmark for future algorithmic improvements, confirming that any further speed‑up must come from exploiting additional structure beyond low Kraus rank.

Quantum channel tomography (also known as quantum process tomography) is a fundamental task in quantum information and quantum computing, aiming to learn the full description of an unknown quantum channel from black-box queries. For channels with input dimension $d_1$, output dimension $d_2$, and Kraus rank at most $r$, [CGO+26] identifies the dilation rate $τ=rd_2/d_1\geq 1$ as a key parameter governing a Heisenberg-to-classical transition in query complexity. While the optimal bounds in the boundary regime ($τ=1$) and the away-from-boundary regime ($τ\geq 1+Ω(1)$) are now known, the precise behavior in the near-boundary regime ($1<τ<1+o(1)$) has remained unresolved. In this paper, we close this gap, thereby fully settling the query complexity of quantum channel tomography. Specifically, we show that the query complexity is - $Ω(rd_1d_2/\varepsilon^2)$ for diamond norm error $\varepsilon$, matching the upper bound by [MB26, CGO+26], - $Θ(d_1^2/\varepsilon+\min\{(τ-1)d_1^2,(τ-1)^2d_1^2d_2^2\}/\varepsilon^2)$ for Choi trace norm error $\varepsilon$. Our results reveal two qualitatively different forms of the Heisenberg-to-classical transition. For diamond norm tomography, the Heisenberg scaling disappears suddenly as soon as $τ$ leaves the boundary regime. In contrast, Choi trace norm tomography exhibits a gradual transition from Heisenberg to classical scaling as $τ$ moves from the boundary regime to the away-from-boundary regime.

In this work, we show that the connection between entanglement and nonclassicality extends well beyond the two-mode mixing setting by considering the case of arbitrary multimode Gaussian evolutions. Using the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as our main technical tool to quantify single-mode phase-space nonclassicality, we derive sufficient conditions for a single-mode state to generate NPT entanglement after a multimode Gaussian unitary evolution, which both tighten and generalize existing criteria. As an application, we obtain simple single-mode protocols for quantitatively testing the entanglement structure of multimode quantum states over arbitrary bipartitions. Our results identify the Narcowich-Wigner spectrum as a powerful tool for investigating fundamental properties of bosonic quantum states.

item.title: Agentic Pipelines for Mapping Topological Codes to Quantum Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it delivers the first formally verified (Lean‑proved) workflow that guarantees a topological error‑correcting code’s low‑energy subspace survives the messy translation from abstract Hamiltonian to real quantum hardware. By coupling AI agents with rigorous verification, the authors can pinpoint and bound unwanted interactions far more tightly than the traditional sum‑of‑strengths approach—crucial for designing devices that meet the stringent gap requirements of fault‑tolerant computing. The method also flags the most problematic qubits and couplings, giving hardware engineers concrete targets for improvement as the field races toward scalable, error‑corrected processors.

Mapping a prescribed many-body Hamiltonian to a particular quantum hardware is generally an approximate process, resulting in both intended and unwanted quantum dynamics. We introduce an AI-agent-assisted workflow that uses Lean to establish whether an effective device Hamiltonian retains the intended low-energy subspace of the target many-body Hamiltonian. We demonstrate this approach with topological quantum error correction (QEC), providing, to our knowledge, the first Lean-verified pipeline connecting a code space to low-energy states of a device model. Starting from qubits and parity checks, the pipeline constructs the ideal Hamiltonian whose lowest energy states form the intended code space, and determines the excitation gap that protects that code space. It then tests if the device retains the required number of isolated low-energy states and quantifies how closely their subspace matches the intended code space. We compare three bounds on unwanted energy shifts obtained by: summing the interaction strengths, grouping the anticommuting Pauli interactions, and diagonalizing the Hamiltonian. Pauli grouping yields a bound that is tighter than the conventional sum and closer to the diagonalization result, avoiding overly conservative compensation requirements. The workflow also identifies the strongest unwanted interactions and the qubits they affect, providing specific targets for improving device couplings and controls. We demonstrate our framework using an eight-qubit toric-code array on a superconducting device, where the same driven device generates both the required four-qubit interactions as well as unwanted dynamics. An AI agent identifies viable device parameters within a prescribed leakage budget, and Lean verifies four isolated low-energy states close to the ideal code space. Our workflow supports predictive hardware engineering for analog implementations of QEC codes.

QYANTRAM addresses this gap through an open platform comprising four subsystems, built around evidence-backed results and independent verification. Its staged compilation pipeline makes every transformation traceable, while the router publishes rejected SWAP candidates and their scores for transparent decision-making. Verification exploits inactive qubits remaining in the |0> state, reducing complexity from 2^N to 2^k for k active qubits. This mathematically exact reduction enables full pre-compilation verification on 127- and 156-qubit layouts, achieving approximately 10,000x speed-ups with execution times below one millisecond. The error identification engine exhaustively evaluates all Pauli error patterns without sampling, matching closed-form predictions within 2.8e-17. Its machine-learning engine achieves numerical agreement within 2.0e-15 of qiskit.quantum_info while training 25-50 times faster. item.description:

Ground states of Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK)-type models are volume-law entangled, which makes them costly both for tensor networks and for quantum hardware simulations. Thus, it remains unclear where quantum hardware could outperform classical simulation of such models. In this work, we study a spin SYK-dot chain, in which q dense SYK dots of p qubits are joined by single ZZ bonds of strength K. The entanglement across any cut is then bounded by floor(p/2) ln 2 plus the inter-dot entanglement, and the two-qubit depth of one Trotter step is set by p alone. A resource estimate shows that a quantum advantage for the ground state could appear only for dots of about 15 to 21 qubits or more. There, a single Trotter step already requires two-qubit error rates of order 10^{-6}, beyond the reach of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. We test the assumptions of this estimate with an imaginary-time matrix product state (MPS) that applies each dot as one block. It agrees with exact diagonalisation at (p, q) = (6, 2). At (5, 2), a variational circuit with the same dot-plus-link layout comes within 3.6% of the exact energy, and noisy simulations show that its fidelity decays as assumed in the resource estimate. At (8, 5), i.e., N = 40 qubits, the energy converges at bond dimension chi = 768, far below the exact value 2^20, and the inter-dot entanglement stays small and is set mainly by K. Out-of-time-order correlators across the links decay on a time scale that shrinks rapidly with |K|. Thus, the dot size p and the inter-dot coupling K together set the entanglement of the chain, and with it where a quantum advantage could appear.

The free particle is the most elementary dynamical system in quantum mechanics. Despite remarkable progress in quantum control of increasingly massive solid-state mechanical oscillators, the analogous control of the free-particle counterpart has remained elusive. Dissipation and environmental noise have prevented such control in the inherently low-frequency domain of free-particle dynamics---a regime of growing importance for quantum sensing and tests of fundamental physics. This is two orders of magnitude below temperatures previously achieved in tabletop optomechanical experiments. We demonstrate immediate utilities of the new operating regime, setting new constraints on modifications of quantum mechanics and benchmarking inferred entanglement-to-decoherence rate ratios nearly two orders of magnitude beyond the state of the art for tests of gravity at the quantum-classical interface.

We evaluate the practical relevance of this abstraction across both simulation and quantum hardware. On quantum hardware, experiments on IBM Heron and IQM Emerald show that which processor is better suited to a given algorithm depends not only on hardware constraints, but also on how well the topology of the quantum algorithm matches the physical connectivity of the processor. These results demonstrate that backend portability is not only a software-design convenience, but can be important for both computational efficiency and quantum execution quality.

AI scientists are expanding automated research across scientific domains, yet their ability to turn the scientific record into a foundation for autonomous discovery remains elusive. Here we uncover a fundamental barrier to this transition and demonstrate a route to overcome it in computational quantum science, where advances shape both what we can learn from complex quantum systems and what quantum computing can ultimately deliver. To identify this barrier, we introduce OmniQ, an expert-audited virtual research environment that converts published studies into executable reproduction tasks. Across 59 papers spanning classical simulation, quantum algorithms and quantum-property characterization, we systematically evaluate five agentic systems powered by large language models and six third-party agent harnesses. Our findings reveal that current AI scientists often fail to reproduce published results, exposing a fundamental mismatch between what scientific papers communicate and what autonomous agents require. By contrast, human expert intervention can turn these failures into successful reproductions, showing that the missing information can be identified and converted into reusable research experience. Guided by this observation, we develop Residual Agents (RA), a quantum-tailored self-improving AI scientist that distils externally verified workflow repairs into such experience. RA substantially improves research performance under fixed base models and limited adaptation budgets. For example, RA raises DeepSeek V4.1 Flash performance from 68% to 85%, matching Claude Code with Opus 5 at a third of its cost despite using a weaker base model. We integrate all reproduced results into an extensible platform built on the model context protocol, making verified research workflows directly accessible to AI scientists and allowing new scientific papers to be continuously incorporated.

item.title: Entanglement inference from quantum erasure and path discrimination
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how to rigorously extract the minimum amount of multipartite entanglement that must have been present in an experiment solely from quantum‑eraser and path‑discrimination data, closing a long‑standing loophole where recovered interference fringes could be misleading. By providing exact semidefinite‐programming bounds and explicit state constructions for noisy GHZ preparations, the work links entanglement certification directly to observable measurement records—a capability that will tighten verification protocols for quantum sensors and near‑term processors. It also clarifies how additional parity or marker measurements can boost certification, offering a practical roadmap for experimental groups seeking device‑independent guarantees without assuming ideal sources. The results therefore sharpen both the theory and practice of entanglement witnessing in hardware‑focused quantum technologies.

Fringes recovered by conditioning on quantum-eraser outcomes do not, by themselves, establish entanglement. We determine the minimum entanglement compatible with recorded eraser data when the preparation may be mixed, distinguishing these data from independently determined optimal which-path distinguishabilities and additional joint measurement outcomes. For noisy Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) preparations, explicit compatible states establish sharp entanglement-depth thresholds and show how parity information strengthens certification. A matching converse establishes the exact threshold for two complete Pauli-outcome distributions. For an ideal three-qubit eraser, we classify the additional marker measurement directions that certify genuine multipartite entanglement within a fixed eraser configuration and determine the separate minima of compatible concurrence and squared GHZ fidelity for specified tilted axes. For noisy three-qubit data, an exact semidefinite characterization and constructive converse determine biseparable compatibility at arbitrary fixed local measurement axes, with rational certificates bounding one example. These results establish what entanglement is required by the measurement record, rather than inferred from assumptions about the source.

item.title: Quantum simulation of dissipative acoustic and elastic waves by Schrödingerisation: absorbing boundaries and explicit polynomial-size circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how to embed simple absorbing “sponge” layers into quantum simulations of acoustic and elastic waves by using Schrödingerisation, turning the inherently dissipative dynamics into a family of unitary circuits that require only one or two auxiliary qubits. By providing explicit polynomial‑size circuit constructions in one, two and three dimensions, it overcomes the closed‑system limitation of earlier wave‑equation simulators and opens the door to realistic modeling of seismic, materials‑science and other wave‑based problems on quantum hardware. The analysis predicts a constant success probability (≈0.4 × the remaining energy) and exact recovery on the truncated auxiliary axis, making the approach compatible with near‑term devices despite the need to manage controlled‑NOT overhead and truncation errors.

Explicit quantum circuits for the acoustic and elastic wave equations, obtained by Hamiltonian simulation of their first-order forms, conserve energy and therefore describe closed domains: an outgoing wave reflects off the edge of the computational region or, with periodic boundaries, wraps around and re-enters from the opposite side. We open the domain with the simplest physical absorber, a graded sponge layer in which every wave field is damped at a rate that grows towards the outer edge, and implement the resulting dissipative dynamics on a quantum simulator by Schrödingerisation, which turns a non-unitary linear evolution into a family of unitary ones by means of a single auxiliary variable. We derive the whole chain from the partial differential equation to the circuit, in one, two and three dimensions. An independent finite-difference solver confirms that damping all wave fields absorbs far better than the common velocity-only damping mask. For the sponge the quantum analysis is sharp: recovery is exact on the whole non- negative half of the auxiliary axis at every time; that axis can be truncated periodically at a length set by the largest damping rate and the simulated time; and the success probability is a fixed constant, about 0.4, times the fraction of the energy not yet absorbed, with only one or two auxiliary qubits measured. On the circuit side, the damping step, which generic synthesis compiles into a number of controlled-NOT gates exponential in the number of qubits, factorises exactly into polynomially many multi-controlled phase gates. Gate-level simulations on up to 25 qubits agree with the classical solutions of the damped wave equations.

item.title: MBUndo: Sound, Automatic, and Efficient Measurement-Based Uncomputation for Quantum Circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces MBUndo, the first automated compiler pass that identifies where ancilla qubits can be safely measured and rewrites their unitary uncomputation into cheap phase‑correction operations, dramatically cutting the costly T‑gate overhead in generic quantum circuits. By extending measurement‑based uncomputation from hand‑crafted examples to any algorithmic design, it dovetails with recent hardware trends that make mid‑circuit measurements fast and reliable, opening a practical path for more efficient fault‑tolerant implementations of large‑scale algorithms such as Shor’s or quantum chemistry simulations. The approach does rely on the availability of low‑latency feed‑forward control, so its full benefit will be realized as those capabilities mature in next‑generation quantum processors.

Quantum programs that use temporary values, known as \emph{ancilla} qubits, must explicitly \emph{uncompute} each ancilla back to zero to ensure that the program produces correct outputs. Conventional uncomputation uses unitary quantum gates, whereas leading quantum algorithms now leverage \emph{measurement-based uncomputation} (MBU), which replaces costly unitary $T$ gates with cheaper measurements and phase corrections. Current quantum programming frameworks can use measurement to uncompute specific gates such as Toffoli. No automatic transformation, however, accepts an arbitrary circuit whose ancillas are computed and uncomputed via the standard approach and converts the circuit to use MBU\@. Researchers instead apply MBU to individual circuit designs by hand, which limits algorithm development and compiler optimization. Such a transformation has not existed due to two fundamental unknowns: where MBU applies and which gates realize MBU for an arbitrary computation. To solve these, we first present a static analysis that identifies, for each ancilla qubit, each circuit position where measurement is sound --- subsuming basic assumptions that MBU only applies at the end of a circuit. Next, we present circuit transformations that soundly turn unitary uncomputation gates into efficient phase corrections after measurement --- generalizing rewrite rules from prior literature that are either limited to a single gate or not applicable to a general circuit. We present \textsf{MBUndo}, an integrated compiler pass that automatically converts circuits to measurement-based uncomputation. It requires no user annotations other than which qubits are ancillas, the same as needed by existing uncomputation synthesizers, and can enhance their output circuits. We evaluate \textsf{MBUndo} on 22 benchmarks to reveal \emph{T} gate reductions of ${>}36.5\%$ over uncomputation synthesizers.
